To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the innate immune system uses a variety of strategies to detect viral infection, (ii) the innate immune response is a highly evolved, multi-layered, and dynamic response to viral infection that is initiated by the detection of viral genomes and replication intermediates, (iii) innate immune responses are initiated by the recognition of unique features of the virus, and (iv) viruses are highly evolved and can evade innate immune detection through a variety of mechanisms.

(1) innate immune sensors detect viral genomes and their replication intermediates; (2) the innate immune system detects viruses that invade the host cell cytoplasm and nucleus by different mechanisms, and (3) viruses that use host cell proteins for their invasion and replication are not detected.

(1) innate immune sensors are designed to detect viral features that are unique to viruses, (2) innate immune sensors have been discovered that can detect viral genomes, replication intermediate and transcriptional by products, (3) innate immune sensors can be activated by viral features other than the genome and viral replication, and (4) there is a need to discover new sensors to cover other viral features that are not yet detected
